newsitem.title: GREECE: Amnesty slams Greece's conscientious objectors law.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty slams Greece's conscientious objectors law.

text.p: Amnesty International, which has long criticised Greece for jailing conscientious objectors, said on Thursday a new law offering alternatives to military service was meant as punishment and would not resolve the chronic problem.

"Amnesty International expresses its sorrow over the government's decision to make the alternative service last twice as long as the military service," the Athens branch of the human rights group said in a statement.

Defence Minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos said on Sunday Greece's estimated 2,500 objectors would be allowed to serve by working in public hospitals or municipal services for double the regular call-up period of 19 months.
"Amnesty International believes that the duration is punitive and will undermine the new measure," the group said.

Greece has often been attacked by international human rights groups for providing no alternative to military service and jailing those who refuse to bear arms -- mostly Jehovah's Witnesses objecting on religious grounds.
Military service is mandatory for all Greek men. Conscientious objectors who evade it cannot get a passport, or work for the public sector and are under the constant threat of being arrested.

Amnesty said that the introduction of the new law was groundbreaking for human rights in Greece but should be enhanced and coupled with the immediate release of about 300 objectors now held in military prisons.

"It is an incomplete measure that does not follow international standards or contemporary perceptions prevalent in other European Union countries and civilised societies in the world," the group said.
It warned that it would continue to campaign for any objectors jailed for refusing to accept an alternative service whose duration is meant as punishment.
